question: Center a div horizontally and vertically using Flexbox (and show the Grid alternative). Assume a `.container` wrapping a `.box`.
thoughtProcess: Centering both axes is the canonical interview warm-up. With Flexbox I make the container a flex container and use justify-content for the main (horizontal) axis and align-items for the cross (vertical) axis. The container needs a height to center vertically. Grid is even shorter with place-items: center.
lineByLine: `display: flex` makes .container a flex container. `justify-content: center` centers children along the main (horizontal) axis. `align-items: center` centers along the cross (vertical) axis. `height: 100vh` gives the container full viewport height so vertical centering is visible. The box keeps its own size and sits dead center.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS Grid
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Grid's place-items centers on both axes in one line.

alternativeApproaches.title: Absolute + transform
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Useful when you can't make the parent flex/grid; centers via 50% offset minus half the element's own size.

followUps.question: Why use transform: translate(-50%, -50%) instead of margins?
followUps.answer: translate offsets by the element's own size without needing to know it, and it works for unknown/dynamic dimensions, unlike negative margins which require fixed sizes.

followUps.question: Does place-items work in older browsers?
followUps.answer: place-items is shorthand for align-items + justify-items and is well supported in modern browsers; for very old support, set them individually or use flex.

question: Build a responsive card grid that auto-fits as many columns as fit, with a minimum card width, using CSS Grid. Cards live in a `.grid` containing `.card` items.
thoughtProcess: The classic 'responsive without media queries' pattern uses repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min, 1fr)). auto-fit collapses empty tracks so cards stretch to fill the row; minmax sets a minimum card width and lets them grow equally. gap handles spacing cleanly.
lineByLine: `display: grid` activates grid. `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` creates as many columns as fit: each is at least 240px and at most an equal fraction (1fr) of the leftover space. auto-fit expands tracks to fill the row when there are fewer items. `gap: 1rem` spaces rows and columns. The layout reflows automatically as the viewport changes — no media queries needed.

alternativeApproaches.title: auto-fill instead of auto-fit
alternativeApproaches.explanation: auto-fill keeps empty tracks rather than collapsing them, so cards don't stretch to fill a sparse last row.

alternativeApproaches.title: Flexbox with wrap
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Flexbox can approximate this but requires basis math and won't equalize widths as cleanly.

followUps.question: What is the difference between auto-fit and auto-fill?
followUps.answer: auto-fit collapses empty columns so existing items stretch to fill the row; auto-fill preserves empty columns, leaving gaps if items don't fill the row.

followUps.question: Why minmax(240px, 1fr) instead of a fixed width?
followUps.answer: minmax guarantees a minimum readable width but lets cards grow to evenly share extra space, keeping the grid fluid.

question: Create a sticky footer that stays at the bottom on short pages but is pushed down by long content. Layout is body > header, main, footer.
thoughtProcess: The robust modern approach makes the body a flex column at min-height 100vh and lets the main content flex-grow to fill remaining space, pushing the footer to the bottom. On long pages the footer flows naturally below the content.
lineByLine: `display: flex; flex-direction: column` stacks header/main/footer vertically. `min-height: 100vh` ensures the body is at least the full viewport tall. `flex: 1` on main makes it absorb all leftover vertical space, so the footer is pushed to the very bottom when content is short. With lots of content, main grows beyond the viewport and the footer simply follows below, scrolling normally.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS Grid
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Grid with 1fr middle row achieves the same without touching main's flex.

alternativeApproaches.title: position: sticky
alternativeApproaches.explanation: `position: sticky; bottom: 0` sticks the footer to the viewport bottom while scrolling, which is a different behavior (always visible) than a pushed-down footer.

followUps.question: Why min-height instead of height: 100vh?
followUps.answer: height:100vh would cap the body at the viewport, clipping or scrolling oddly with long content; min-height lets it grow.

followUps.question: Is the Grid or Flex approach better?
followUps.answer: Both are valid; Grid with grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto is arguably the cleanest and doesn't require styling the middle element.

question: Make columns equal height regardless of their content. A `.row` contains several `.col` elements with varying text.
thoughtProcess: Equal-height columns were painful before flexbox. Now, flex children stretch to match the tallest sibling by default via align-items: stretch. I just make the row a flex container; each column fills the row's height automatically.
lineByLine: `display: flex` lays columns in a row. `align-items: stretch` (the default cross-axis behavior) makes each column expand to the height of the tallest one, giving equal heights for free. `flex: 1` on each .col makes them share width equally. `gap` spaces them. Content of any length now produces uniformly tall columns.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS Grid
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Grid rows stretch items to the row height by default, also yielding equal heights.

alternativeApproaches.title: Legacy: display: table
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Before flexbox, table-cell siblings shared height; rarely used now.
alternativeApproaches.code:
.row { display: table; width: 100%; }
.col { display: table-cell; }

followUps.question: What if I want inner content (like a button) pinned to the bottom of each equal-height column?
followUps.answer: Make each .col a flex column with `flex-direction: column` and push the button down with `margin-top: auto`.

followUps.question: Does stretch override an explicit height?
followUps.answer: No — if a column has its own height, stretch won't override it; remove fixed heights to let stretch work.

question: Truncate a single line of text with an ellipsis when it overflows its container.
thoughtProcess: Single-line truncation needs three properties working together: the element must not wrap (white-space: nowrap), must clip overflow (overflow: hidden), and must show the ellipsis (text-overflow: ellipsis). It also needs a bounded width to overflow against.
lineByLine: `white-space: nowrap` forces the text onto one line so it can overflow. `overflow: hidden` clips the part that exceeds the box. `text-overflow: ellipsis` renders the clipped end as '...'. A bounded width (`max-width`) is required — without a size constraint there's nothing to overflow, so no ellipsis appears.

alternativeApproaches.title: Truncate inside a flex item
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Flex children won't shrink below content size by default; add min-width: 0 so ellipsis works.

followUps.question: Why isn't my ellipsis showing inside a flexbox?
followUps.answer: Flex items have an implicit min-width:auto that prevents shrinking below content; set min-width: 0 on the truncating item.

followUps.question: Can text-overflow: ellipsis work without overflow: hidden?
followUps.answer: No — text-overflow only applies to content clipped by overflow; you need overflow other than visible.

question: Clamp text to a maximum number of lines (e.g. 3) with an ellipsis (multi-line truncation).
thoughtProcess: Multi-line clamping uses the webkit line-clamp mechanism, which is widely supported despite the vendor prefix. It requires display:-webkit-box, a box orientation of vertical, the line-clamp count, and overflow hidden. The newer standard `line-clamp` is emerging but the -webkit set remains the cross-browser solution.
lineByLine: `display: -webkit-box` opts into the flexible box model that line-clamp hooks into. `-webkit-box-orient: vertical` stacks the lines vertically so clamping by line count makes sense. `-webkit-line-clamp: 3` limits visible text to 3 lines and adds an ellipsis. `overflow: hidden` clips the rest. The unprefixed `line-clamp` is the standardizing property and is included for forward compatibility.

alternativeApproaches.title: max-height fallback
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When line-clamp is unsupported, cap height to line-height * N with overflow hidden (no ellipsis, but it bounds the text).

followUps.question: Why does line-clamp still need the -webkit- prefix?
followUps.answer: It originated as a non-standard WebKit feature; browsers implement it under -webkit- for compatibility while the standard `line-clamp` matures.

followUps.question: Can you clamp and keep a 'Read more' link inline?
followUps.answer: Not reliably with line-clamp alone; you typically overlay a gradient/fade and a separate button, or use JS to measure and insert the link.

question: Build a custom toggle switch from a checkbox. HTML: a label wrapping an `<input type="checkbox">` and a `<span class="slider">`.
thoughtProcess: The trick is to visually hide the real checkbox (keeping it accessible/functional) and style a sibling span as the track, with a ::before pseudo-element as the knob. Then use the :checked state via the sibling combinator to move the knob and recolor the track. Transitions make it smooth.
lineByLine: The input is hidden with opacity:0 (not display:none, so it stays focusable/operable). `.slider` is the rounded track. `.slider::before` is the circular knob positioned at the left. The adjacent-sibling selector `input:checked + .slider` recolors the track when checked, and `+ .slider::before` slides the knob with translateX (a composite-only transform, so it animates smoothly). Transitions animate both color and knob position.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use accent-color for a quick native toggle
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For simple needs, a native checkbox recolored with accent-color is far less code, though not a sliding switch.

followUps.question: Why opacity:0 instead of display:none for the input?
followUps.answer: display:none removes it from the accessibility tree and tab order; opacity:0 (often with sized/positioned input) keeps it keyboard-focusable and clickable through the label.

followUps.question: How do you make the switch keyboard accessible?
followUps.answer: Keep the real checkbox in the DOM and focusable, associate it with the label, and add a visible :focus-visible outline on the slider when the input is focused.

question: Build a responsive navbar that shows links inline on desktop and stacks them on mobile. HTML: nav > .brand + ul.links (with li > a).
thoughtProcess: Desktop-first: lay links out horizontally with flexbox and space them from the brand. Then a media query at a mobile breakpoint switches the link list to a vertical stack. This is the CSS layout half; a real toggle button would need JS/checkbox, but the layout shift itself is pure CSS.
lineByLine: The nav is a flex row with brand and links pushed apart by space-between. `.links` is a horizontal flex list with gap spacing and reset list styling. The media query at 640px switches both nav and links to vertical (flex-direction: column), stacking the brand above a full-width vertical link list — the responsive transformation, done purely with CSS.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS-only collapsible menu
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A hidden checkbox toggles the menu's visibility via :checked, giving a hamburger menu with no JS.

followUps.question: How would you add a hamburger button without JS?
followUps.answer: Use a hidden checkbox and a <label> as the button; toggle the menu with the :checked state via a sibling combinator.

followUps.question: Mobile-first vs desktop-first here?
followUps.answer: Mobile-first (base = stacked, min-width query adds the row) is generally preferred for performance and progressive enhancement.

question: Create a box that always maintains a 16:9 aspect ratio regardless of width.
thoughtProcess: Modern CSS makes this trivial with the aspect-ratio property: set the ratio and a width, and height follows. I'll also show the classic padding-top hack for older browser support, which leverages the fact that percentage padding is based on width.
lineByLine: `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9` tells the browser to compute height as width * 9/16 automatically. `width: 100%` makes it fill its container; height then derives from the ratio. Resize the container and the box keeps a perfect 16:9 shape. No wrappers or hacks required.

alternativeApproaches.title: Padding-top hack (legacy)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Percentage padding resolves against width, so padding-top:56.25% yields a 16:9 box; absolutely position the content inside.

followUps.question: Why does padding-top: 56.25% give 16:9?
followUps.answer: 9 / 16 = 0.5625; percentage vertical padding is computed from the element's width, so the height equals 56.25% of width — a 16:9 ratio.

followUps.question: Does aspect-ratio work with images/video?
followUps.answer: Yes — it's especially useful to reserve space and prevent CLS for media before it loads.

question: Build a modal overlay with a dimmed backdrop, centered content, that prevents background scrolling. HTML: .overlay > .modal.
thoughtProcess: The overlay is a fixed full-viewport layer with a semi-transparent background; centering its child is a flexbox job. A high z-index keeps it above page content. Preventing background scroll is typically done by adding overflow:hidden to the body (often via a class toggled in JS); the CSS provides that class.
lineByLine: `position: fixed; inset: 0` stretches the overlay across the whole viewport. The `rgba` background dims the page. Flexbox centers the modal. `z-index: 1000` lifts it above page content. The modal caps its width/height and scrolls internally with overflow:auto if content is tall. `body.modal-open { overflow: hidden }` disables background scroll while the modal is open (the class is toggled when opening/closing).

alternativeApproaches.title: Native <dialog> element
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The HTML <dialog> with showModal() provides a built-in backdrop (::backdrop), focus trapping, and Esc-to-close with minimal CSS.

followUps.question: Why use inset: 0 instead of top/right/bottom/left: 0?
followUps.answer: inset is the shorthand for all four offsets; inset:0 pins the element to all edges of its containing block in one declaration.

followUps.question: How do you trap focus inside the modal?
followUps.answer: Use the native <dialog> (auto focus trap) or JS to keep Tab focus within the modal and restore focus to the trigger on close.

question: Create a CSS-only tooltip that appears on hover using a ::after pseudo-element. HTML: a `.tooltip` element with a `data-tip` attribute.
thoughtProcess: I'll generate the tooltip bubble from the ::after pseudo-element, pulling its text from the data-tip attribute via attr(). It's positioned absolutely relative to the hovered element (which needs position: relative), hidden by default, and revealed on :hover with opacity. A transition makes it fade in.
lineByLine: `.tooltip { position: relative }` makes it the positioning context for the bubble. `content: attr(data-tip)` injects the tooltip text from the HTML attribute. Absolute positioning with bottom:125% places the bubble above the element, and left:50% + translateX(-50%) centers it horizontally. `opacity: 0` hides it; `pointer-events: none` prevents it from blocking the mouse. On `:hover` the opacity goes to 1, and the transition fades it in.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add an arrow with ::before
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A second pseudo-element styled as a CSS triangle (transparent borders) gives the tooltip a pointer.

followUps.question: Why is pointer-events: none important on the tooltip?
followUps.answer: Without it, the bubble can intercept hover/clicks and may cause flicker or block the element underneath.

followUps.question: Is a CSS-only tooltip accessible?
followUps.answer: Not fully — it isn't announced to screen readers and isn't keyboard-triggerable. For accessibility, use a real element with aria-describedby and show on focus too.

question: Build a loading spinner using @keyframes animation. HTML: a single `<div class="spinner">`.
thoughtProcess: A classic spinner is a circle with a transparent border except one colored side, rotated continuously. I make a square with border-radius:50%, give it a light full border and a single contrasting border-top, then animate an infinite 360-degree rotation with transform — which is GPU-friendly and smooth.
lineByLine: The 40x40 box becomes a circle via border-radius:50%. A 4px light gray border forms the ring; overriding `border-top-color` with blue makes one segment stand out so rotation is visible. `animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite` runs the keyframes forever at constant speed. The `@keyframes spin` only needs a `to` rotating 360 degrees — animating transform keeps it on the compositor for smooth motion.

alternativeApproaches.title: Dual-ring / dots variant
alternativeApproaches.explanation: You can animate multiple pseudo-elements with staggered animation-delay for dot spinners.

alternativeApproaches.title: Respect reduced motion
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Disable or slow the animation for users who prefer reduced motion.

followUps.question: Why animate transform: rotate instead of other properties?
followUps.answer: transform is composite-only, so the spin runs on the GPU compositor thread and stays smooth even if the main thread is busy.

followUps.question: How do you respect users who dislike motion?
followUps.answer: Wrap or override the animation under @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to slow or stop it.

question: Create gradient (multi-color) text. HTML: a heading element with a class `.gradient-text`.
thoughtProcess: The standard technique paints a gradient as the element's background, then clips the background to the shape of the text and makes the text fill transparent so the gradient shows through the glyphs. This uses background-clip: text (with the -webkit- prefix for broad support) and text-fill-color.
lineByLine: `background: linear-gradient(...)` fills the element's background box with the gradient. `background-clip: text` (plus the -webkit- prefix) clips that background to the glyph shapes. `-webkit-text-fill-color: transparent` makes the actual text color see-through so the clipped gradient shows through; `color: transparent` is the fallback for engines without text-fill-color. The result is text painted with the gradient.

alternativeApproaches.title: Animated gradient text
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Make the gradient larger than the text and animate background-position for a shimmering effect.

followUps.question: Why include both -webkit-text-fill-color and color: transparent?
followUps.answer: text-fill-color (prefixed) is what WebKit/Blink honor over color; color:transparent is the fallback for engines that support background-clip:text but not text-fill-color.

followUps.question: Any accessibility concern with transparent text?
followUps.answer: The text is still real and selectable/readable by screen readers; just ensure the gradient maintains sufficient contrast against the background for sighted users.

question: Animate a hamburger icon (three bars) into an X using CSS. HTML: a button with three `<span>` bars, toggling a `.open` class.
thoughtProcess: The three bars become an X by rotating the top and bottom bars 45 degrees in opposite directions and hiding the middle bar. To make them cross at the same point, I rotate the outer bars and translate them toward the center; the middle fades out. Transitions animate the morph. The .open class (toggled by JS or a checkbox) drives the state.
lineByLine: Each span is a 24x3 bar with vertical margins, and transitions on transform and opacity so changes animate. When `.open` is applied: the first bar moves down (translateY) and rotates +45deg; the middle bar fades to opacity:0; the third bar moves up and rotates -45deg. The two outer bars cross at the center forming an X, while the transitions make the change a smooth 0.3s morph. Removing `.open` reverses it back to three bars.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS-only with a checkbox
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Drive the state with a hidden checkbox's :checked instead of a JS-toggled class.
alternativeApproaches.code:
#nav-toggle:checked + .hamburger span:nth-child(2) { opacity: 0; }
#nav-toggle:checked + .hamburger span:nth-child(1) { transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg); }

followUps.question: Why translateY before rotate matters?
followUps.answer: transform order is applied right-to-left in effect; translating then rotating positions the bars so they intersect at the center — different orders shift the pivot and misalign the X.

followUps.question: How do you keep this accessible?
followUps.answer: Use a real <button> with aria-expanded reflecting the open state and an accessible label like 'Toggle menu'.

question: Implement dark mode using CSS custom properties (variables). HTML: a root element that gets a [data-theme="dark"] attribute.
thoughtProcess: Define semantic color variables on :root for the light theme, then override them under a [data-theme="dark"] selector. All components reference the variables (var(--bg), var(--text)) so flipping the attribute re-themes the whole app with no per-component changes. I'll also show automatic OS preference via prefers-color-scheme.
lineByLine: :root defines the default (light) values for semantic tokens. The `[data-theme="dark"]` block redefines those same variables with dark values; because components read `var(--bg)`/`var(--text)`, toggling the attribute on the root cascades new colors everywhere instantly. body and links consume the tokens rather than hard-coded colors, so theming is centralized in one place.

alternativeApproaches.title: Follow OS preference automatically
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use prefers-color-scheme so the theme matches the user's system setting without a toggle.

alternativeApproaches.title: Smooth theme transition
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a transition on color/background for a gentle switch.

followUps.question: Why use semantic variable names like --bg instead of --white?
followUps.answer: Semantic names (--bg, --text) describe purpose, so the value can flip between themes without the name becoming a lie like '--white' holding a dark color.

followUps.question: How do you combine a manual toggle with OS preference?
followUps.answer: Default to prefers-color-scheme, but let a [data-theme] attribute (set via JS, persisted in localStorage) override it when the user explicitly chooses.

question: Build the Holy Grail layout (header, footer, and three columns: fixed-width left nav, fluid center, fixed-width right aside) using CSS Grid.
thoughtProcess: The Holy Grail layout was notoriously hard before Grid. With grid-template-areas I can describe the entire page visually: a header and footer spanning full width, and a middle row with three named columns. grid-template-columns sets fixed side widths and a flexible center (1fr). I'll add a responsive collapse for mobile.
lineByLine: `display: grid` with `min-height: 100vh` makes the page at least full height. `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px` fixes the side columns and lets the center flex. `grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto` sizes header/footer to content and lets the middle row grow. `grid-template-areas` draws the layout as ASCII art, and each section claims its region with `grid-area`. The media query at 700px collapses everything to a single column and reorders the areas into a mobile stack.

alternativeApproaches.title: Flexbox version
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Achievable with nested flex containers (column outer, row middle), but ordering source vs visual position and equal heights are clumsier than Grid.

followUps.question: Why is Grid better than Flexbox for Holy Grail?
followUps.answer: Grid is two-dimensional: it positions rows and columns simultaneously and lets you reorder regions independent of source order via template areas, which Flexbox can't do as cleanly.

followUps.question: How does source order vs visual order affect accessibility?
followUps.answer: grid-area can place a visually-central main while keeping it logical in the DOM; keep DOM order sensible for screen readers and tab order, since CSS reordering doesn't change focus order.
